Topic:Gambling

Sun 5 Jul 2026 at 5:00am

There should be rules against jumping on the World Cup bandwagon to illustrate a political point, but the Socceroos' valiant effort against Egypt offers a timely real-world test. (ABC News: Monty Jacka)

There should be rules against jumping on the World Cup bandwagon to illustrate a political point, but the Socceroos' valiant effort against Egypt offers a timely real-world test.

The live television broadcast featured two advertisements for gambling in the minutes before kick-off, including the promotion of lucrative odds on a "same day multi" bet for the game watched by millions of Australians.

For those who slept through their alarms and were left to catch up via streaming would also have seen plenty of wagering ads.

The interesting question is what Labor's bill to restrict gambling ads would change?

And the answer in this case is, not a whole lot.

Due to the 4am kick off, gambling ads would still be permitted right up to the scheduled start of the match, at the half time break and immediately after the final whistle for normal time.

As it transpired, the nail biting extra 30 minutes of play and devastating penalty shootout pushed the finish time beyond 6am, which under the new laws would trigger an ad blackout during scheduled breaks and straight after the game.

During play there would be no ads or wagering discussions allowed at all, including the promotion of live odds.

But Australians catching up later via streaming could be served such ads at any time unless they were under 18 or had selected the "opt-out" button on the platform.

The most notable difference would be that no celebrities — including sport stars — could feature in any of the promotions.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese this week declared the federal government's plan gets the "balance" right, but there are MPs even in his own ranks who are far from sure about that.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese this week declared the federal government's plan gets the "balance" right, but there are MPs even in his own ranks who are far from sure about that. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Labor's proposal includes a crackdown on overseas online gambling sites and lotteries, bans ads in stadiums and on player uniforms and prohibits the use of celebrities and social media influencers in any promotions.

Live broadcast restrictions are tougher between 6am and 8.30pm than outside those hours when children are presumed not to be watching.

The Albanese government will target social media influencers and individuals who promote gambling on social media as part of its proposed laws.

For example, had the Socceroos' started playing at 4pm ads would be banned in the five minutes before and after the game, during play and at half-time on live TV.

It's the latitude on timing, along with the opt-out model for online advertising, that has fuelled criticism the laws do not go far enough.

Concerns over such details have already driven the Greens and Coalition to team up and send the bill to an eight-week inquiry for further scrutiny, prompting warnings from Communications Minister Anika Wells this would only delay meaningful action.

Albanese's problem is two things can be true at once.

Labor's laws are the strongest ever proposed in Australia, but they do not completely cover all the harms many people expected the government to address.

Australians have many records to be proud of, but their status as the world's biggest gambling losers per capita is not one of them.

Some $32 billion is lost annually, according to an Equity Economics report commissioned by anti-gambling advocates last year.

More than a third of that money is gobbled up by poker machines, a point Albanese has emphasised as he this week argued the government wanted to tackle problem gambling without stopping overs who want to "have a punt".

While the pokies have long been a source of concern, in recent years scrutiny of online gambling and sports betting has increased considerably.

The issue was expected to feature prominently at Labor's national conference later next month, with cynics inside the party arguing Albanese only moved in April to avoid this.

Evidently, the draft bill published this week has not completely neutralised internal concerns.

Inner West Sydney Mayor Darcy Byrne (the man many believe would replace Albanese in his seat of Grayndler when the PM retires) has focused his attacks on pokies, but also on Friday acknowledged the federal government's bill might need a "second stage" to "strengthen" the laws.

The reforms heavily rely on online platforms deploying technology like age assurance, account-based viewing and opt-out settings.

If those systems work well, Labor can rightly argue children and self-excluded users would receive far fewer, if not zero gambling ads.

But the extent to which social media giants, streamers and podcast platforms will comply with the laws, let alone prominently promote the opt-out option, is currently a complete unknown.

The push for Labor to go further is coalescing around a few key concerns, including extending the broadcast ad ban to all live sport and targeting so-called gambling "inducements" like bonus bets.

Liberal MP Simon Kennedy has led the charge against what he has characterised as a "carve-out" for streamers, which are subjected to the online rules rather than TV restrictions.

Streamers need to take steps to ensure under 18s do not receive gambling ads, while adults must have the option of an "opt-out".

But they are not required to limit the volume or type of ads they otherwise show.

SBS On Demand already has an opt-out button for gambling ads on its platform, but as Kennedy points out, surveys have found only about 0.2 per cent of people have been able to find it.

This column counted two wagering ads during a 30-minute highlight of the Portugal vs Croatia match viewed via the streamer on Friday.

There were nine ads that ran for about 3.5 minutes total during the replay, meaning gambling promotion accounted for roughly a third of the total advertising time.

Wherever Labor's final laws land, Peta Murphy certainly would not have envisioned gambling ads playing during the World Cup. (ABC News: Luke Stephenson)

The debate around gambling harm reduction is, understandably, an emotional one.

Firstly, there are the heartbreaking stories of addiction that have destroyed lives and torn families apart — research has found a typical problem gambler negatively affects about six close individuals.

For many MPs, particularly on the Labor benches, tackling the issue also carries an additional personal meaning due to the initial work of the late Peta Murphy.

Murphy, a beloved Labor MP who passed away in 2023 after a battle with breast cancer, had chaired the inquiry into online gambling that resulted in the You Win Some, You Lose More report that partially informed Labor's bill.

Wells paid tribute to her friend when introducing the legislation, while Murphy's name — and legacy — is frequently invoked by those who say the reforms are not enough.

Albanese has sought to balance the concerns of free-to-air broadcasters, sporting codes and those who argue a domestic crackdown would merely send Australian gambling dollars abroad.

Wherever Labor's final laws land, Murphy certainly would not have envisioned gambling ads playing during the World Cup.
